questions.stem: Where is the heart's natural pacemaker located?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The ventricle contracts; it does not set the tempo.
The aorta is an exit vessel, not a rhythm setter.
The septum separates sides; the pacemaker sits in the right atrium.

questions.stem: What do pacemaker cells send out to start a contraction?

options.explanation: The signal is electrical, later becoming mechanical.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Adrenaline is hormonal; the pacemaker works electrically.
Oxygen arrives by blood, not from the pacemaker.

questions.stem: In what unit is heart rate expressed?

options.explanation: That is a flow volume, not a beat count.
That unit measures blood pressure.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Far too slow a unit for a living pulse.

questions.stem: What role does the pacemaker play in keeping the beat?

options.text: It filters the blood passing through
options.explanation: No filtering happens in the atrium.

options.text: It stores oxygen for the muscle
options.explanation: Storage is not a heart role.
Adrenaline comes from glands, not the pacemaker.

options.text: It regulates the heart rate and coordinates the contraction of the cardiac muscle
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Which two factors are named as raisers of the heart rate?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Sleep lowers the rate; hydration has no such effect.
Neither is the named pair here.
Calm states leave the resting rate untouched.

questions.stem: State where the pacemaker sits and what it does.
questions.modelAnswer: It sits in the right atrium and coordinates the contraction of the heart muscle, regulating the heart rate.
It is the number of times the heart beats in a minute.

questions.stem: Explain why impulses from one region keep the heart beating in an orderly sequence.
questions.modelAnswer: Because every contraction is initiated from the same pacemaker, the electrical spread follows a fixed route, so atria and ventricles contract in the proper order.

questions.stem: An athlete's resting rate sits at 50 beats per minute. Use the pacemaker idea to explain what a coach measures.
questions.modelAnswer: The coach is counting the beats per minute set by the athlete's pacemaker; a low resting value reflects an efficient pump rather than a faulty conductor.

questions.stem: Why do muscle cells need a faster blood supply during exercise?

options.text: Blood supplies them with adrenaline only
options.explanation: Adrenaline is a signal, not the muscle's fuel.

options.text: They respire faster, demanding more oxygen and glucose and quicker waste removal
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They stop respiring to save energy
options.explanation: Respiration accelerates rather than stops.

options.text: They need less oxygen when active
options.explanation: Activity raises the demand, not lowers it.

questions.stem: Which two responses does the heart make during exercise?

options.explanation: No pausing occurs during exercise.

options.text: It pumps less per beat to save energy
options.explanation: Per-beat volume increases, not decreases.

options.text: It beats faster and pumps a larger volume per beat
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Slowing would starve the muscles.

questions.stem: Why does heart rate stay high after exercise ends?

options.explanation: Cooling is not the named reason.
Adrenaline fades; the debt is the driver.
The muscles are recovering, not resting, during this period.

options.text: To supply the oxygen that breaks down the lactic acid built during the oxygen-free route
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: What may muscle cells do when oxygen supply cannot meet demand in intense exercise?

options.text: Add anaerobic respiration alongside the still-running aerobic route
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Energy demand continues; cells never stop.
Animal cells cannot photosynthesise.

options.text: Store glucose instead of using it
options.explanation: Storage would starve the contraction.

questions.stem: How does adrenaline raise the heart rate?

options.text: By slowing digestion to a stop
options.explanation: Digestion changes, but the rate rises through the pacemaker.

options.text: As the hormone behind fight or flight, readying the body for sudden action
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Walls do not thicken on demand.

options.text: By adding glucose to the blood directly
options.explanation: Adrenaline signals; it is not a fuel.

questions.stem: State what the heart supplies to respiring muscles and removes from them.
questions.modelAnswer: It supplies oxygen and glucose for respiration and removes carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Name the hormone that raises heart rate without exercise.
questions.modelAnswer: Adrenaline, the fight-or-flight hormone, lifts the heart rate ahead of action.

questions.stem: Explain why both heart rate and per-beat volume must rise together in exercise.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the muscles' faster respiration needs more oxygen and glucose delivered per minute, and one mechanism alone could not move enough blood to meet that demand.

questions.stem: A sprinter's pulse is still high two minutes after finishing. Explain the physiology.
questions.modelAnswer: The sprint added anaerobic respiration in the leg muscles, building lactic acid; the raised heart rate supplies the oxygen needed to break that lactic acid down, repaying the oxygen debt.
